title: The wetland's missing rain
blurb: The Pantanal lives on its floods. Is rainfall over it falling?
narrative: Open the case: rainfall over the Pantanal, Brazil, since 1981.
Check the evidence: the yearly series, its trend line and both tests.
Call the line-up: did evaporation, clouds and sunlight change with it?
Look at the map: where around the wetland does the trend hold?

variable.name: Precipitation
variable.definition: How much water falls from the sky as rain or snow, on an average day.

emergence.explanation: The trend first became statistically clear in 1999, when the record was 19 years long, and it has stayed clear ever since.

verdict.headline: Case closed: precipitation is falling.
verdict.how_much: -0.333 mm/day per decade (Sen's slope); the fitted line changes by -1.29 mm/day over the whole period (-48%).
verdict.how_sure: Both tests agree this is very unlikely to be chance (t-test p < 0.001, Mann-Kendall p < 0.001).

limitations: Values come from MERRA-2, a global reanalysis (a weather model corrected with observations), on a grid of roughly 50 km: they describe the area around the point, not the exact spot.
Only straight-line trends are tested. A change that speeds up, slows down or reverses is not captured.
The tests treat each year as independent of the one before. No correction for year-to-year correlation is applied.
A trend shows that a value changed, not why it changed.

variable.name: Water vapour in the air column (CERES)
variable.definition: All the water vapour in the air above one square metre of ground, from the CERES satellite data product.

variable.name: Cloud thickness
variable.definition: How much the clouds block light passing through them. Higher means thicker clouds.

variable.name: Cloud cover
variable.definition: The share of the sky covered by clouds.

variable.name: Sunlight reaching the ground
variable.definition: The energy from the Sun that reaches the ground, clouds included.

variable.name: Precipitation
variable.definition: How much water falls from the sky as rain or snow, on an average day.

variable.name: Evaporation from land
variable.definition: How much water leaves the land surface and goes back into the air.

variable.name: Surface brightness (albedo)
variable.definition: The share of sunlight the ground reflects back. Snow and sand are bright, forests and oceans are dark.

variable.name: Ground surface temperature
variable.definition: How warm the surface of the land or sea itself is, not the air above it.

variable.name: Air temperature
variable.definition: How warm the air is about 2 metres above the ground, averaged over day and night.

variable.name: Heat radiated down by the sky
variable.definition: The invisible heat radiation that the air and clouds send down to the ground.

variable.name: Deep soil wetness
variable.definition: How wet the whole soil layer is, from the surface down to bedrock. 0 is dry, 1 is soaked.

variable.name: Sunlight under a clear sky
variable.definition: The energy from the Sun that would reach the ground if there were no clouds. It changes when the air gets hazier or cleaner.

variable.name: Topsoil wetness
variable.definition: How wet the top 5 cm of soil is, from 0 (completely dry) to 1 (soaked).

variable.name: Root-zone soil wetness
variable.definition: How wet the top metre of soil is, where plant roots drink. 0 is dry, 1 is soaked.

variable.name: Relative humidity
variable.definition: How full of water vapour the air is, compared with the most it could hold.

variable.name: UV index
variable.definition: How strong the Sun's skin-burning ultraviolet rays are at the ground.

variable.name: Temperature swing
variable.definition: The gap between the hottest and the coldest hour of the day, on average.

variable.name: Hottest temperature
variable.definition: How hot the hottest hour of the day gets, 2 metres above the ground, on average.

variable.name: Moisture in the air
variable.definition: Grams of water vapour in each kilogram of air near the ground.

variable.name: Dew point
variable.definition: The temperature at which the air would become saturated and dew or frost would form. Higher means muggier air.

variable.name: Water vapour in the air column (model)
variable.definition: All the water vapour in the air above one square metre of ground, from a global weather model.

variable.name: Wind speed
variable.definition: How fast the air moves 10 metres above the ground.

variable.name: Coldest temperature
variable.definition: How cold the coldest hour of the day gets, 2 metres above the ground, on average.

variable.name: Haze (aerosol optical depth)
variable.definition: How much dust, smoke and pollution particles in the air block sunlight. Higher means hazier air.

variable.name: Air pressure
variable.definition: The weight of the air pressing down on the ground.

variable.name: Ozone layer
variable.definition: The total amount of ozone in the air above, the gas that shields us from ultraviolet rays.

variable.name: Wind speed higher up
variable.definition: How fast the air moves 50 metres above the ground, the height of a wind turbine.

variable.name: Frost days
variable.definition: How many days were cold enough for frost to form (air below 0 °C).

variable.name: Snow depth
variable.definition: How deep the snow lying on the ground is.

variable.name: Snow cover
variable.definition: The share of the land covered by snow, from 0 (none) to 1 (all).

variable.name: Snowfall
variable.definition: How much water falls as snow over land, on an average day.

lineup.summary: 19 of 27 tested variables show a significant trend after correcting for the number of tests. 4 variables had too little data to test.

variable.name: Precipitation
variable.definition: How much water falls from the sky as rain or snow, on an average day.

summary.text: Of 336 cells tested, 20 cells are rising significantly and 240 cells are falling significantly.

opposite_twin.text: Same variable, same years, opposite direction: +0.338 mm/day per decade at (-23.5, -57.5) against -0.826 mm/day per decade at (-15, -53.75), 1023.7 km apart.
